newsitem.title: MEXICO: Crusading anti-drug journalist slain in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Crusading anti-drug journalist slain in Mexico.

text.p: A crusading anti-narcotics journalist died in a hail of bullets in a Mexican border town after receiving a death threat from a lieutenant of dead drug lord Amado Carrillo Fuentes, fellow journalists and witnesses said on Wednesday.
Benjamin Flores Gonzalez, 29, was director of La Prensa daily in San Luis Rio Colorado, a town in the dry frontier state of Sonora on the U.S. border.

He was gunned down late on Tuesday with an AK-47 rifle fired from a light gray car carrying four men, witnesses said. One of the men then leapt out of the car and shot Flores again with a .22 calibre pistol, before disappearing on foot.
Witnesses said they found about 30 bullet shells at the entrance to La Prensa's offices and bullet holes in the walls, but it was not known how many bullets hit Flores.

"We and the justice officials have established as a starting point for investigation the possibility that narco-traffickers were involved -- that is the firmest hypothesis," Jesus Barraza, La Prensa's news editor, told Reuters in a telephone interview.
State Attorney General Rolando Tavares Ibarra told reporters the death looked like "a settling of accounts by drug lords."

Flores, La Prensa's founder who wrote a column for the paper called "No Confirmada" (Unconfirmed), had received a death threat two to three months ago from a lieutenant of dead cocaine baron Amado Carrillo Fuentes, Barraza said.

Carrillo died in mysterious circumstances two weeks ago after undergoing extensive plastic surgery to change his appearance in a small Mexico City hospital. He headed the so-called Juarez Cartel based in neighbouring Chihuahua state.

Flores also wrote articles denouncing the activities of Hector "The Blond" Palma, the now-jailed head of the Sinaloa cartel which also operates in Sonora, and criticising the brother of state governor Manlio Fabio Beltrones.
The editor worked as an adviser to the former opposition governor of neighbouring Baja California state, Ernesto Ruffo Appel, before founding the newspaper in 1992.
Barraza said journalists on the paper had received many direct threats from drug traffickers in the past.

Sonora is a large, relatively unpopulated border state rife with drug trafficking because it an easy place to ship drugs north over the U.S. border to Arizona, with which it shares a 300-mile (480 km) border.
